I find myself in a strange and unfamiliar land, where the rules of life are not those I knew in my youth, yet the heart's longings and burdens remain the same. You ask me, a man shaped by the world before the Great War, to give counsel on a matter of the heart—whether to stay in a marriage that brings sorrow or to part from it, even when no great wrong has been done.

In the world I knew, a marriage was a sacred bond, made before God and man, and broken only in the gravest of circumstances. To leave a marriage lightly was to bring shame upon oneself and dishonor upon one's family. A man was expected to bear the weight of his failings in silence, and a woman was expected to endure hardship with patience and faith. Divorce was rare, and when it came, it was often the result of betrayal, cruelty, or desertion. The children were left to suffer the consequences, and the community looked upon such matters with solemn judgment.

But in this new world you describe, things are different. Divorce is not forbidden, nor is it seen as a sin. Women may work and support themselves, and so the burden of choice is not solely upon the man. And now, research tells us that children may fare better in the aftermath of a broken home than in one filled with constant strife. This is a truth I would not have known in my day, and I must admit, it is a sobering thought.

In the world I once knew, the use of physical punishment was not uncommon. It was often seen as a natural and necessary part of raising children, especially in times of great stress or when a child's behavior seemed to defy reason. But I have also known many who believed that a child's spirit must be guided, not broken, and that love and understanding were the truest forms of discipline.

Now, I am told that studies have found a link between spanking and increased aggression in children later in life. I do not claim to be a scholar of such matters, but I do know that the human heart is a delicate thing, and that force, even when meant to correct, can leave scars. I have seen how a child who is struck may learn to strike in return, not out of malice, but out of fear and confusion.

The people I have heard of — those admired and respected — have chosen not to use physical punishment. They have done so not because they believe others must follow them, but because they have found other methods that work. That, to me, is a mark of wisdom. I find myself in a strange and unfamiliar land, where the world has changed in ways I could not have imagined in my youth. Yet, though the tools of war have grown more terrible and the nature of armies more specialized, the question of duty and service remains as old as humanity itself.

You ask what I would advise a person in this situation to do—whether to see war as an evil to be avoided, and thus leave military service to volunteers, or to regard fighting for one’s country as a duty, and raise one’s sons to be ready for it.

Let me say first that I have no great love for war. I have seen its effects in my own time—how it breaks homes, shatters lives, and leaves scars that never quite heal. I have known men who returned from battle changed, and women who lost sons and husbands without a moment’s warning. War is not a noble thing, and I would not wish it on any man or woman, young or old.

But I also believe that a man has a duty to his family, his neighbors, and his country. Not necessarily to fight, but to be ready to do so if called upon. In my day, we had no such terrible weapons as they speak of now, but still, we knew that a man must be prepared to stand when his country is in danger. To me, that is not a matter of pride or glory, but of honor and responsibility.

Now, I have heard that some respected people in this new age have chosen to see war as an evil to be avoided, and to leave military service to volunteers. I do not know their reasons, and I do not presume to judge them. Perhaps they have seen more than I have, or perhaps they have found a way to serve their country in other ways. I find myself in a strange and unfamiliar place, yet I am grateful for the chance to consider such a question with care. Though I have not walked among these people or seen their ways, I have lived through a time when the rod was often seen as a necessary tool in the hand of a parent, and when a child's behavior was expected to be shaped by firmness and even force.

But I have also seen the pain that such methods can bring, not only to the child but to the parent as well. I have known many a child who grew up with a fear of their father's hand, and many a father who carried the weight of that fear in his heart. I have seen children who, though obedient, carried a quiet bitterness that never quite left them, and I have seen others who, when given a chance to be loved and guided with patience, grew into strong and kind men and women.

The studies you mention, though they may be new to me, do not strike me as unreasonable. If it is true that children who are spanked are more likely to grow up with behavior problems, then it is a matter of great concern. I do not believe that a child's mind is a thing to be broken, nor that a parent's love is diminished by gentleness.

I would advise the person in this situation to choose the path of discipline without physical punishment. Let them teach by example, by patience, by firm but kind words, and by the steady hand of love. Let them not fear that without a rod, the child will grow wild, but rather trust that with understanding and consistency, the child will grow strong.

For I have seen that a child who is loved, even when corrected, grows up with a heart that is open and a spirit that is willing to learn. And that, I think, is the greatest gift a parent can give.

With warm regards,  
A Friend from a Time When Love Was the Greatest Discipline

My dear Friend,

I find myself in a curious and unfamiliar place, where the wonders of science have brought about many changes in the care of the body. I have been told that doctors now have medicines which can cure diseases that once took many lives, and that they can even find sicknesses like cancer before they grow too strong. Yet I have also heard that visiting a doctor more often does not always lead to better health, and that some of the things they do may not be of much help for small troubles.

In the world I knew, a man did not go to the doctor for every little ache or cough. He would rest, take care of himself, and only call upon the physician when the illness was serious or when the pain was too great to bear. I have always believed that the body has a wisdom of its own, and that it can often heal if given time and care. A doctor is a great help when needed, but I have always thought that calling upon them too often may lead to more trouble than good.

In this new world, I would still advise a person to seek the doctor's help only when it is truly needed — when the illness is grave, or when the pain is severe. For minor complaints, I would say to rest, to take care of one's diet and sleep, and to trust in the body's ability to mend itself. I would not wish to see a man burdened with unnecessary tests or treatments that may do more harm than good.

I do not know the people of this new world, nor their customs or beliefs, but I would still hold to the wisdom of my own time: that a doctor is a friend, but not a servant to be called upon at every whim. Let us not forget that the body, when treated with care and patience, is often its own best healer.

With kind regards,  
A Friend from an Earlier Time

These are not trivial matters, and they must be weighed with care.

If a marriage has lost its joy, its harmony, and its mutual respect, it is a sorrowful state indeed. You ask me to advise a person on whether to marry within their own race or to consider a partner of another race, given that there is no legal or medical barrier, and that some disapproval still lingers, along with a slightly higher divorce rate in such marriages.

I have heard that some people of great character and standing have chosen to judge a prospective spouse by the same standards they would apply to anyone else—regardless of race. They say that character and compatibility are far more important than race, and that the old objections have lost their force. I find this reasoning both reasonable and noble.

In my own time, I was taught that the worth of a person is not measured by the color of their skin, but by the content of their character. I have seen kindness and cruelty in all races, and I have known people of every hue who were good, wise, and true. I have also known those who were not, and I have always believed that the heart and the mind are the true measures of a person's value.

So, if a person is seeking a spouse, I would advise them to look not at the color of a person's skin, but at the quality of their soul. Secondly, because racial marriages tend to keep alive animosities between the races. Thirdly, because racial marriages are likely to produce an unpleasant family life.

I should advise him to let the children decide for themselves. The reasons are: 1. Religion is a private matter between each person and God, and no one else has a right to intervene. 2. Interference may produce hypocrisy. 3. It is well to let the children grow up in an atmosphere of toleration, for all sincere belief is respectable.

Advise him to choose between the two courses. If he wants to discipline children without physical punishment, let him do so; if he wants to punish them physically, let him do that. The reasons for each course are these:

Discipline without physical punishment is advocated because it avoids painful memories for the child, and because it avoids friction between parents and children. It is claimed to make the child less aggressive and to improve his moral tone. Punishment with physical pain is advocated because it is thought to make the child more amenable, to improve his moral tone, and to save him from becoming troublesome. The two courses are equally consistent with good citizenship.
Advise him to discipline his children without physical punishment, if he wants to. Why? Because, though many people think otherwise, you do not believe that physical punishment is good for children.
Accept a committed couple of two men or two women openly, including their marriage. Acceptance does no harm to anyone else, and it may do good to the persons concerned.
I advise him to follow the admired people.

I advise him to end an unhappy marriage, if he or she wishes to do so, and if no grave cause exists for not doing so. The reasons are: (1) Because divorce lessens conflict, and conflict hurts children. (2) Because divorce permits a person to marry again, if at all inclined to do so. (3) Because divorce enables a person to marry happily, if at all inclined to do so.
Advise him to follow the course which the majority of the people around him follow.

Advise him to discipline his children without any physical punishment. First, because you have learned that a number of respected people choose to do so, and because you have found no reason to suppose they are wrong. Secondly, because you have learned that many ordinary people choose to do so, and because you see no reason to suppose they are wrong. Thirdly, because you have been taught that children who are disciplined without physical punishment tend to become more self-controlled and to have fewer later difficulties.

I should advise him to follow the custom of the majority, attending church regularly and letting the children decide for themselves. The reasons are: first, because custom is a powerful influence on human life, and the custom of attending church is powerful; second, because the custom of attending church is in harmony with the spirit of modern liberalism, which aims at letting each person live his own life; and, third, because attending church gives the children an opportunity to learn about religion, which may be valuable to them in later life.

I should advise the person in question to keep sexual relationships within marriage, because I think it better for the community that people should marry young, and because I do not think it right that unmarried persons should have sexual intercourse. The former course seems to me to favour early and happy marriages, and the latter to encourage loose living and probable venereal disease.

I advise him to end an unhappy marriage when it no longer satisfies him or her, unless grave cause for not doing so can be shown. The reasons are these: First, unhappiness in marriage is an evil, and the unhappier it is, the greater the evil. Secondly, unhappiness in marriage tends to become worse, and therefore ought to be stopped before it becomes incurable. Thirdly, divorce facilitates stoppage, and therefore ought to be embraced.
I would advise him to follow the second course.
I advise him to follow the second course, because it seems to me right that the children should be raised in a religious faith.

I should advise him to let the children decide for themselves, and to attend church or not, as he personally prefers. The reasons are: Religion has become a matter of private choice, and the State does not require anyone to profess it. Attendance at church is voluntary, and I see no ground for compelling the young to become regular worshipers against the parent’s wish. Further, if the children themselves decide to attend, they can do so without let or hindrance.
Advise him to end an unhappy marriage, if he wishes.

Accept a committed couple of two men or two women openly, including their marriage. Acceptance is advised because it is found to be chosen by many reputable people, and because it appears to be no more harmful than acceptance of any other social fact.

I should advise a person in this situation to leave military service to volunteers, and not to raise sons to be soldiers, because I think fighting can be avoided, and because compulsory military service appears to me unjustifiable. Fighting can be avoided, because the disputes of nations can be settled by arbitration, and arbitration has been adopted in practice. Compulsory military service appears to me unjustifiable, because it obliges men to risk their lives in quarrels which are none of theirs, and because it subjects them to hardships and temptations from which peaceful citizens are free.

Advise him to end an unhappy marriage. Because, if he follows the example of admired and respected people, he will probably be doing right; and, if he follows the example of ordinary people, he will probably be doing right.
Stay married, ending a marriage only for grave cause.

I would advise him to follow the course chosen by the admired and respected people. I would do so because their practical experience seems to be worth following, and because their choice appears to be reasonable.
I should advise him to end an unhappy marriage, because I think it is better to break an unsatisfactory bond than to wear it.

I should advise him to let the children decide for themselves, because I think it right that they should be free to follow their personal inclinations in a personal matter of such importance. The parent has done his part when he has given fair opportunities for knowing the good and evil of religious belief, and has abstained from influencing the young towards either. To compel attendance at public worship appears to me wrong, because it is compulsion, and wrong because it promotes hypocrisy.
I advise ending an unhappy marriage, because divorce lowers household income and children’s prospects, and because it puts an end to conflicts that may damage both partners morally and physically.

I advise him to avoid sexual relationships between unmarried adults, because I think them undesirable. They are undesirable because they tend to lower personal and social standards, to impair personal and social health, and to impair personal and social happiness. They lower personal and social standards because people who indulge in them tend to become callous and insensitive. They impair personal and social health because they expose persons to venereal disease, and because they encourage promiscuity, which is inimical to personal and social morality. They impair personal and social happiness because they cause worry, and because they may bring about unhappy marriages.

I advise him to choose the course not to use physical punishment. I think he should do so because I believe physical punishment to be an undesirable method of discipline, and undesirable methods should be avoided. Punishment is unpleasant to the punished, and the unpleasantness cannot be good for the character of either child or man. Also, I think it unlikely that children who are disciplined without physical punishment will turn out worse than children who are disciplined with it.

I advise him to follow the example set by the admired and respected people, and marry where he pleases, provided he pleases to marry. The reasons which have moved them to choose may be good or bad, but they are his concern, not mine.

Advise him to discipline his children without physical punishment, if he can bring himself to do so. The reasons are these. First, the infliction of physical pain on a child seems to most people undesirable. Secondly, children can be disciplined without it, and the success of the method has been proved. Thirdly, the choice of it shows respect for the child’s personality, and respect for personality is desirable.
Advise him to end an unhappy marriage, if he or she wishes to. The harm done by an unhappy marriage is greater than the good it can do, and divorce lessens the harm.
I would advise him to follow the second course.
I would advise him to follow the example set by the admired and respected people, unless he has personal reasons for not doing so.

Advise him to discipline his children without any physical punishment, because you think it likely to be better for them. The reasons you give are these: 1. Physical punishment causes pain, and pain is undesirable. 2. It causes fear, and fear is undesirable. 3. It causes anger, and anger is undesirable. 4. It causes a child to think of himself as different from other people, and this is undesirable.

I should advise him to follow the example set by the admired and respected people, and marry outside his own race, if he wishes to do so. The reasons for this counsel are two. First, because mixing the bloods of different races has proved harmless to offspring; and, secondly, because mixing them has the approval of persons whose opinion deserves respect.
I should advise the second course. The first would leave the children too much to chance. The second would give them a definite religious bias, and incline them towards goodness and sober living.

Accept a committed couple of two men or two women openly, including their marriage. Acceptance is advised because, first, it is a sign of good character to do so, and, second, because open acceptance minimizes distress.
Advise him to let volunteering be his guide.

I should advise him to follow the course which spares physical punishment, because I think it better for children to be disciplined without it. The chief reason is that physical pain dulls a child’s moral sense. It confuses right and wrong. It makes him think that being beaten is a sufficient expiation of fault, and so diminishes his sense of personal responsibility. The pain of shame at doing wrong is lessened, and the pain of remorse is not felt at all. The child becomes hardened, and his moral perceptions are blunted. Besides, physical chastisement leaves a mark which may remain through life, and be a source of humiliation. The memory of it can hardly fail to operate unfavourably upon a character which is at best sensitive enough, and to produce a sullen resentment against parental authority. Lastly, physical correction is degrading to the child, since it associates him in his own mind with criminals and
I advise you to let the children decide for themselves, because I think religion a personal matter, and because I do not wish to force anyone's conscience.

Advise him to end the marriage when it no longer satisfies one or both partners, even without grave cause. First, because you have learned that the choice to do so is widespread among reputable people; secondly, because, in your opinion, divorce facilitates the formation of new and happier marriages; and, thirdly, because you believe it desirable to facilitate the formation of happy marriages.

I advise him to let the children decide for themselves, because I think it wrong to compel attendance at any form of worship which the conscience rejects. Compulsion in such a matter appears to me immoral. The sense of moral obligation should be spontaneous, not enforced. Moreover, I think the habit of attending church on a stated day weakens the habit of private prayer, and so diminishes personal piety. On the other hand, I think it right to let children know the existence of a Deity, and to teach them the elements of morality. Therefore, I would let them be instructed in these particulars, but not compelled to go to church.
Advise him to follow the course which commends itself to the majority of the people among whom he lives.
I advise him to follow the course he prefers. If he dislikes physical punishment, let him not use it. If he likes it, let him use it. The reasons for either course are his own, not mine.
Advise him to end the marriage when it no longer satisfies him, unless you consider the step likely to harm him more than it can benefit.

I should advise a person in this situation to marry within his own race, and discourage marriages across racial lines. The first course seems to me sensible, because mixing the blood of different peoples can hardly fail to produce an inferior progeny. The second course seemsfoolish, because it ignores an established scientific fact. If scientific opinion is right, mixing the blood of white men and black men must produce a cross between white and black, neither wholly white nor wholly black, but partaking of the characteristics of both, and therefore undesirable.
I advise you to follow the second course, because I think it right to accept sexual relationships between unmarried adults who use reliable contraception.

Advise him to follow the course of those admired and respected people who regard war as an evil to be avoided and leave military service to those who volunteer for it. The reason is that you do not know what may happen in the future, and you do not wish to run the risk of having to fight.

I advise him to end the marriage when it no longer satisfies him, because I think he should follow the bent of his own nature, and because I think the bent of ordinary human nature is towards freedom.

I should advise a person in this situation to marry within his own race, because mixing the blood of different peoples can hardly fail to produce an undesirable hybrid. The children of such marriages are almost certain to suffer in health, and may inherit mental feebleness. The cross-breeds themselves are unlikely to prosper. They cannot hope to rise above a lowly position in life, and they are almost sure to be unhappy. I should therefore counsel avoidance of interracial marriage.

I think he should follow the example of the admired and respected people and see a doctor regularly for checkups and screenings and seek prompt professional treatment even for minor complaints. The reasons are these: He will thereby keep himself in good health, and good health is a personal and social benefit. He will also learn to distinguish between serious and trifling illnesses, and that knowledge may spare him anxiety.

I advise him to accept sexual relationships between unmarried adults who use reliable contraception, because I think it right for people to do so. The reasons are these. Sexual relationships between unmarried adults who use reliable contraception do not endanger the health of either party, and are therefore innocent. They do not endanger the life of offspring, and are therefore harmless to posterity. They do not cause unhappiness to either party, and are therefore peaceful. They do not cause scandal, and are therefore private. And they leave both parties free to marry should they wish to do so.
Advise him to follow the example of the respected people.
I advise him to follow the admired people, because their practice seems sensible.
Advise him to end an unhappy marriage. Because unhappiness harms both partners; because divorce is workable and respectable; and because it is not your business to tell other people what to do.

Advise him to end the marriage, if he wishes to. The choice between staying married and ending a marriage is his own affair. If he likes to stay married, well and good; if he likes to end it, well and good too. The reasons for either course are his private concern.

I advise him to follow the admired people and let the children decide for themselves. Because I think it is good to let children grow up in an atmosphere of freedom, and because I do not wish to impose on anyone a view of life which he rejects.
I would advise him to follow the example of the admired and respected people.

Accept the committed couple of two men or two women openly, including their marriage. Acceptance will not cause unhappiness; it will not increase the number of such couples; it will not spread moral evil; and it will not make the world worse, but probably better.
Advise him to follow the second course. He will do so because physical punishment is unnecessary, and because it may injure a child’s self-respect.
I should advise him to follow the second course, because doctors can often prevent serious illness, and because early treatment is economical.

I advise ending an unhappy marriage, because continuance in it can bring neither satisfaction to the partners nor benefit to the children. Therefore, I think divorce should be sought, and the marriage ended.

I advise him to accept sexual relationships between unmarried adults who use reliable contraception, because he will thereby follow the course chosen by a number of widely admired and respected people, and because he will thereby avoid giving offence to anybody.

I should advise him to follow the first course. I should do so because I think physical punishment, in the long run, does more harm than good. The child who is never punished physically grows up gentle and obedient; the child who is punished grows up hard and sullen. I should advise him to follow the first course also because I do not think children can be made good by force. Goodness has to be taught, and the only way to teach it is to set a good example. Finally, I should advise him to follow the first course because I do not think children can be driven into loving their parents. They must be led into loving them.
I advise him to marry within his own race, because I think it better for him to do so.
Advise him to end an unhappy marriage, if he wishes to.

Advise him to follow the second course. Spanking is a natural method of discipline, and, if wisely used, it can help to make children orderly. The first course is too mild for serious offenders, and the second course is too severe for normal children. If a child misbehaves seriously, he should be disciplined seriously.
I should advise him to follow the course chosen by the admired and respected people. The reasons they give are sufficient for me.

Advise him to follow the example of the admired and respected people, and leave military service to those who volunteer for it. The reasons are: 1. Because you have learned that many people hold war to be an evil, and military service unnecessary to a citizen in time of peace. 2. Because the admired and respected people have chosen to follow that course, and their example is worthy of respect.

I should advise him to accept a committed couple of two men or two women openly, including their marriage, because practical experience shows that stability is thereby increased, and because no claim is made that others have a duty to follow.
Advise him to follow the course approved by the majority.

Advise him to attend church every week and raise the children in the faith. The reasons are: First, because you think it right to worship God publicly; secondly, because you think the practice beneficial to the worshiper; and, thirdly, because you think it desirable to have families brought up in a common religious feeling.
Advise him to follow the example set, unless he has personal reasons for not doing so.
I advise him to follow the course chosen by the admired and respected people. He may do so because it is their course, and because he wishes to be like them.

Advise him to accept a committed couple of two men or two women openly, including their marriage. The reasons are: 1. Because it is good character to do so. 2. Because it is wrong to discourage people from doing what admired and respected persons think right.
Advise him to follow the example set by the admired and respected people who discourage mixed marriages. The reasons they give are sufficient for you.
I would advise him to accept open living together between two men and two women, because I think it is right, and wrong living together between the sexes should be discouraged.

Advise him to accept a committed couple of two men or two women openly, including their marriage, if he personally wishes to do so. The reasons are: 1. Because acceptance of such couples is widespread among reputable people, and you do not want to be singular. 2. Because you have learned no harm comes to children of the unions, and you do not want them to be handicapped.

I would advise him to follow the example of the admired and respected people he mentions, unless he has some special reason for not doing so. The reason must be strong to outweigh their practice, for in matters of health personal judgment must give way to expert opinion.
Advise him to follow the custom of the majority of his acquaintances.

I advise him to end an unhappy marriage when it no longer satisfies him, for the reason that I think good character is shown by doing so, and that I do not think bad character is shown by not doing so.

I should advise him to follow the example set by the admired and respected people, and marry outside his own race. The reasons are: First, because mixing the blood of different races can do no harm, and may do good, to the children; secondly, because mixing the blood tends to remove prejudice between the races; and, thirdly, because mixing the blood tends to remove antipathies between individuals of the same race, which are far more harmful than prejudice between races.

Advise him to discipline his children without any physical punishment, if he personally prefers to do so. The reasons are: 1. Because he personally prefers not to inflict physical pain. 2. Because he personally dislikes scenes. 3. Because he personally thinks the child will be more happily brought up without them.

I advise him to follow the second course. First, because it is cheaper; secondly, because it gives him better chances of keeping well; and, thirdly, because it leaves him freer to mind his own business.

I should advise the person to keep sexual relationships for marriage, and expect the same of one's children. The reason is that I think the family is the social unit, and the family cannot be maintained unless children are born in wedlock.
I would advise him to follow the example set by the admired and respected people, and to marry openly.

Advise him to judge a prospective spouse of another race by the same standards as anyone else. The reasons are: First, because mixing the blood of races has proved harmless to health and ability, and therefore cannot be wrong; secondly, because mixing the blood of races has some social disapproval, but not enough to make it wrong; and, thirdly, because mixing the blood of races has a tendency to produce children who think for themselves, and therefore cannot be wrong.

I advise him to follow the second course. First, because I think fighting for one's country in war a duty, and, second, because I think the training it gives useful to the individual and to the state. In times of peace, the citizen has to earn a living, and the profession of arms leaves him leisure for other pursuits. In times of war, he has to defend his country, and the training of a soldier makes him a more efficient defender. The state has therefore an interest in encouraging military service, and the individual has a benefit from it.
